utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a couple of preliminary matters before the witness is brought in. In view of the nature of some of the testimony to be given by this witness, the Prosecution applied for protective measures of delayed disclosure and use of a pseudonym. Those measures were granted by the Chamber on the 3rd of May, 2002. The witness having now attended to testify in The Hague has informed the Prosecution that he no longer requires any protective measures or a pseudonym during his testimony and will be testifying, or it would be his wish to testify in open court. We therefore seek a variation of your earlier order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The second matter, Your Honour, is the Prosecution, with respect to a video that it intends to tender with this witness, had applied for certain measures or protective measures regarding that video which had been provided to the Office of the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 70. By a decision of the 7th of June, 2002, the Chamber ordered that, one, the video and the accompanying transcript be identified as B3000 in all court documents; two, the identity of the provider not be revealed; three, the submission of the video and the transcript as an exhibit be done under seal; and four, any Court session in which the video may be shown be a closed session and that the video feed and transcript not be made public. Since those orders were made, the provider of this video has agreed that the video may be shown publicly. The Prosecution therefore requests that your orders, the first, third, and fourth order of your decision of the 7th of June be varied to enable the public showing of this video and the public display of the transcript. As the provider still wishes to remain anonymous, the Prosecution is requesting that your second order remain in effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, just for the record, Mr. Milosevic raised a statement. I believe he misspoke when he said a statement created the 17th of February, 1993, as it appeared in the transcript. The statement was signed by this witness on the 17th of February, 2003. It was turned over to Mr. Milosevic on the very day, an hour after it was signed. I will not be asking any questions regarding that statement. The history -- the brief history of the statement is it was the result of an interview that began some time ago, but because this witness in large part was travelling, it was unable to be completed until he arrived in The Hague. It was provided to Mr. Milosevic in terms of completeness but, again, I will not be asking any questions regarding the contents of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution now calls Mr. Dragan Vasiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While he's being brought, we've been given three separate binders of documents. They're numbered 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I take them to be the exhibits which this witness will be producing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first one -- the first tab on number 1 is the proofing summary. That, of course, will not be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Although no doubt we could exhibit the others in due course. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're discussing exhibits, it would be helpful to assign exhibit numbers to those three binders. The first one would be general exhibits, the one you've just referred to. The second one would be exhibits associated with the video. And the third binder are exhibits associated with the Captain Dragan fund.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take the numbers for those.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Binder number 1, Your Honours, is Prosecutor's Exhibit 389; binder number 2 is Prosecutor's Exhibit 390; and binder number 3 is Prosecutor's Exhibit 391.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In the first of those, as I said, 389, the first tab, which is the summary, will not be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just before I begin, during the presentation of the evidence here today, we will be using, in conjunction with the standard way that we've been tendering evidence, just a computer programme to facilitate the quick presentation of the evidence. I've put an explanation of it at the beginning of the witness summary. I've also -- depending on what participant and where you're sitting in the courtroom, you need to push a different button on your console to have access to that, and there is a chart on the witness summary to indicate to all participants here what button they should push to see this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to please begin by telling us your name.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Vasiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber how it was you came to be a witness in this case and your motivation for testifying here today.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: There are four reasons why I'm here. For me, this was a major decision. The first is that in the indictment against the accused, my name is mentioned. Also, quite a number of witnesses have mentioned my name here in the courtroom. Some did it in giving the chronology of events in Krajina, and some did so tendentiously, to distort the truth, so that by coming here I hope I will be given the chance by the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber, the accused to convey the full truth. And the third reason, of which I'm sure you're aware, there is a great deal of scepticism towards this Tribunal, and I share that scepticism, but I think that all of us who participated in those events should come here and make our statements so that one day, if justice is not served, people will have material on which to rely. Another motive, major motive, I must say that in the last five years I have had to answer questions -- the question as to whether an indictment has been issued against me over the past five years. I speak not only on my own behalf but on behalf of many witnesses who have been here, and I think this is a big problem. So by coming here, if there's anything against me, if there is an indictment against me, I'd be told about it, so I can continue my life normally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, what is your understanding of whether or not there is any agreement between yourself and the Office of the Prosecutor regarding your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing except to present the truth here. That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there ever any offer of some indemnity or immunity from Prosecution offered to you at any time in your dealings with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I said on the very first day that I did not need any protection. I was given a piece of paper which I didn't wish to sign in which it says that whatever I say here cannot be taken against me, but I didn't want to sign that because I feel that I don't need any kind of protection from this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 389, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there a letter of proffer provided to you in the last week in your preparation for testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the letter. As you see, I did not sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is your understanding of the effect of this letter of proffer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think this is a letter that says that whatever I may say in the preparation for this trial or during the trial against the accused cannot or will not be used against me. And I take full responsibility for everything I did and for whatever I'm going to say here, so I see no reason why I should sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was that letter provided to you in anticipation of putting allegations to you that the Office of the Prosecutor had from other sources, allegations of possible wrongdoing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what your motive for this is, but probably it is as you say. But as I have already said, I really don't need any kind of protection, and therefore, this one either. And I wish to respond to any accusations that may be made against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you to look at the screen in front of you. I'm going to ask that Mr. Vasiljkovic's monitor be placed to "Off." I'm going to ask that you look at 389, tab 1. It should be on the monitor in front of you. Do you recognise what's depicted in that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: The letters are very small. If they could be magnified, please. Oh, yes, I see. This is a description of my educational background and experience prior to my arrival to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In order to save time, I will not go into detail of your background. Are you willing to answer additional questions, either by the accused or the Chamber, should they wish?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To begin your testimony, I would like to ask you just to briefly describe a number of persons who you will refer to during the course of your testimony. Could you please tell us who Frenki Simatovic is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Frenki Simatovic is a member of the state security service, the first man I met from that service in Yugoslavia, who later became my family friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is he your personal friend to this day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic is also a member of the state security service. When I met him, I don't know what position he held, but he was a senior officer in that service, and as far as I know, he was a superior to Frenki Simatovic to a high degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us your understanding of what the state security service is. What branch of government does it come under, and what is its mandate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: When I got in contact with the service, though later on it was changed and I can't say much about that with precision, but when I got in contact with it, it was kind of a secret service, like many other secret services in the world the task of which was to protect the constitution, and in that period it was subordinated to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Ministry of Interior of Serbia or the Federal Ministry of Interior of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian service was subordinated to the Serbian Ministry of the Interior, and the federal service was subordinated, I think, to the Federal Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. -- or Major Fico Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time I met him, he was a lower-level member of the service who worked as a partner or an associate of Frenki Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Radonjic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Radonjic was also one of the associates of Frenki Simatovic who later, much later, became head of the municipal service of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know, briefly, about Mr. Dusan Orlovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Dusan Orlovic is a very quiet, charming gentleman who in that time -- at that time was head of the state security service of Krajina, of the Krajina secret service that was in the process of being formed at the very beginning. I had several encounters with him at the beginning. Later on, I had very little occasion to meet him, but I do know that he held the position of head of the secret service of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Sasa Medakovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Sasa Medakovic was a member of the Krajina service. Later, he became my friend, and actually, he was the person who took me down to Krajina, and it was through him that I received most information about developments in Krajina, and he helped me make the decision to go to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Srba Milovanov.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Srba Milovanov is a colleague of mine, a pilot like me, and I know him from the air force days. Later he became a member of parliament -- I'm sorry, a member of parliament in the Serbian parliament, and he introduced me to Frenki Simatovic and the service down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, a person by the name of Mark Lynch.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Mark Lynch is also a colleague of mine, a pilot, a former member of the Red Berets of the British army who, on my invitation, came to assist me to set up a training camp in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, is it true that for a period of your life you lived and worked in Australia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I spent most of my life in Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And while in Australia, were you a member of the armed forces or the Australian defence forces reserve?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For approximately how many years were you a member of those defence forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: For six years. I was an active member of the defence forces of Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you may have come to Yugoslavia on a number of occasions. What I want to ask you at this point is did you return to Belgrade in May of 1990?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't come there from Australia. I came from America on my private plane, a small single-engine aircraft with which I landed in Belgrade without planning to stay at all. I was on my way to Africa, and Belgrade was just a stop-off, and I waited for the suitable conditions for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. me to continue my flight to Tanzania, which was my destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At this time in May of 1990, can you characterise for us your understanding or lack of understanding of the political developments in Yugoslavia at that time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I was brought up in a Yugoslav spirit. Zagreb, for me, was my town, the Adriatic was my sea, my best man is a Croat. I don't know -- there is a statement in our language, a saying that says, "God comes first and then the Kum," or the best man. That is how important a Kum is among the Serbs. So I didn't understand it properly. I gathered it was a post-Titoist era of unrest in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. And later I started to experience it as a resurgence of revanchism in Croatia with the strengthening of the HDZ which was reviving the Ustasha policies most aggressively. That was my understanding. But to tell you quite frankly, I didn't know there was an area called Krajina, nor that it was inhabited by Serbs when I arrived in May 1990. Another important point: When I was crossing over the Atlantic, the first place I landed in was Rijeka in Croatia. So I had absolutely no prejudices as to what was going on in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that soon after your arrival in Belgrade you were the subject of some attention because you had flown a single-engine aircraft across the Atlantic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not just that. Several years before that, that is 1993 to 1996 -- no. I must correct myself. In 1983, I left Australia on a lovely yacht of 28 tonnes that I had built myself. Then I cruised on it along the oceans, and I arrived in Yugoslavia in a yacht. So believe me, there are very few Serbs to have achieved anything like that. And especially when I crossed over the Atlantic in a single-engine plane, it wasn't difficult to find friends there, and I aroused quite a bit of interest at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video that the Prosecution will tender and ask the Chamber to watch the entirety of is 48 minutes long, so I'm going to interrupt this portion of the questioning and move ahead to section 4 of the witness summary - that's paragraph 52 - so that the showing of the videotape does not go into the break, and then I'll return to this afterwards. I do have some preliminary questions to ask Mr. Vasiljkovic in advance of showing that video. Mr. Vasiljkovic's monitor should be set to "Off" for him to see it as well. It will not be shown on the video channel but on the computer evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljkovic, did you attend a ceremony in 1997 which celebrated the history of the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's when I got a type of medal from that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did you arrive at that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I, a lady friend of mine, Frenki Simatovic, and a lady friend of his arrived by helicopter from the Military Medical Academy to the place where the camp was, of the unit for special operations, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was Mr. Milosevic present during the course of that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you be shown Prosecution Exhibit 390, and this is tab 1. It's a video cassette. I'm just going to ask that the witness be shown the physical copy of the cassette. After you arrived here in The Hague, were you asked to view a videotape on a television?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm very impressed. I have to tell you a few things in connection with this tape. I asked if I could get a copy of this tape. I was told that I could not because this is very sensitive material. On this tape are absolutely all members of the Serb service. I believe that in the history of secret services, security services, this is a unique case, that you have all the members of a security service on one single tape. So I really wanted to have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt we shall see it in due course. Could you, if you would, confine yourself just to answering the questions you're asked so we can get on more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The physical cassette that you see in front of you, after you viewed the videotape, was the cassette taken out and presented to you for you to sign to memorialise that that is the video that you viewed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are your initials contained on the label of that video cassette?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next exhibit, which doesn't concern the witness, at least this portion of it, would be tab 2, and that would be the official CLS copy of both the Serbo-Croatian text or speech and the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljkovic, were you offered or given a copy of the Serbo-Croatian transcript as well as the English transcript of the video, of this tape?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And having been actually present there, did you identify some errors in the tape, especially with respect to the identity of some of the people who were present?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that you take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 390, tab 4. There's a -- two different transcripts there. Are those the transcripts that you corrected?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the course of viewing this videotape, were there some veterans of the conflict in Krajina, men that you had personally trained and been associated with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 390, tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you, with a member of the Prosecution staff, create a chart listing the names of the veterans as well as the time on which they appear on the videotape?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You made this, and I corrected some of the mistakes that -- the grammatical mistakes and others that were obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the exhibit before you now is the chart of the veterans and people that you were associated with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, I'd ask that the witness be shown --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- Prosecution Exhibit 390, tab 5, and ask you, similarly, did you also view some stills taken from the video and assist a member of the Prosecution staff in identifying the people there so that the Chamber may know who the different people are that appear during the course of the video?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of these people are public figures and everybody knows them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you initial the bottom of each of those pages to indicate that the identifications of those stills are accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'm going to ask that the exhibit be played. At the conclusion of it, I will ask the witness a few questions regarding it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For the record, you would give the number of the exhibit so we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So I would be asking that 390, tab 1, be played, although I will note that what the Court will actually see is a digitised version of that video as well as a version of the transcript, and as the Court will see, the computer programme will move the transcript along with the video so that the Chamber can relate the two. It should be on everybody's monitor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Please refer to Exhibit 390 tab 2 for video transcript]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the 1987 parade, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: 1997, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 1997, sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, the video that we have just watched, did it fairly and accurately depict the events as you remember them at the ceremony you attended on that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there any significant portion of the ceremony that was not depicted on this video that you think, in fairness, you would like to describe for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Whoever was filming this I think did a very good job, and I think he covered all the most important parts of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in advance of the break, Mr. Nice would like to address the Chamber in private session regarding another witness. Perhaps, if it's convenient with the Court, we would excuse Mr. Vasiljkovic at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vasiljkovic, we're going to deal with some other matter which doesn't concern you at all. If you'd like to go now. We're going to adjourn for 20 minutes. Would you remember in this break and any others there may be during your evidence not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that includes the members of the Prosecution team. If you'd like to go now and be back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, I want to return to where we were prior to the showing of the videotape. You were describing or you were telling us about your trip or your return to Belgrade in May of 1990, and the question I have for you is: At that time, did you begin to frequent a coffee bar that was frequented by people from the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the time when in the media there was a lot of talk about the situation in the Krajina, and I started going to that place often. Actually, that's where firsthand information was received as to what was going on in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this coffee bar, was it in Belgrade itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during this time period, were you approached by a man by the name of Sasa Medakovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Sasa Medakovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe for us, when you initially met Mr. Medakovic, did he identify his profession or who he was to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. At first he introduced himself to me as one of the defenders of the barricades at that time in the Krajina. Later on, he introduced himself to me as Martic's friend, and finally he introduced himself to me as an employee of the state security service of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: From your conversations with Mr. Medakovic and your conversations with the people of the Krajina at this coffee bar, did you form an impression of what was happening in the Krajina at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We saw each other quite often, practically every day, and I was quite familiar with this, and I learned quite a bit from him about the situation in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe for us or summarise for us what your belief was about the current situation at that time in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw this as an extremist political party, like the HDZ was, coming to power, and it brought about the resurgence of some of the things that had happened during the Second World War. I saw this as a true primeval fear on the part of the Serbs who lived in the area. And I met a lot of people there, and I think that their fear was most sincere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you at some point let it be known that you were willing to go down and assist in the Krajina if your assistance would be beneficial?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I reached that decision only after I visited the Krajina. I didn't know how I could help. But I wanted to go there, and I wanted to see this with my very own eyes, all these things that I heard about in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you did make a visit to the Krajina itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was that year, late in the autumn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So in the autumn of 1990, you made a visit to the Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you went when you went to the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when we arrived in Krajina, we went straight to the office of Milan Martic at the local police station. Do you want me to tell you about this in greater detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before you tell us about that initial -- that meeting with Mr. Martic, can you describe for the Chamber your trip down to the Krajina and anything of significance that you saw.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I went down there with two other friends who are irrelevant to what happened after that in Krajina. On our way to the Krajina, we came across barricades, roadblocks. At these barricades, there were people, civilians in some kind of half uniforms. All of this looked very disorganised. From the point of view of a soldier, I mean, these were not real barriers at all. All of them were placed very unprofessionally. They were guarded by ordinary men, most of the time drunk, and they were quite unorganised. On the road to Knin itself, I saw some of these ugly messages addressed to the Serbs. One remains imprinted in my memory. I remember it to the present day. It said, "I cut the tree trunk and you cut the branches. Ante Pavelic." Now, that is something that I really remember that remained imprinted in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The car that you drove down there, what kind of plates did it have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Belgrade plates. And these Belgrade plates made it possible for us to pass the barricades without any problems whatsoever. People greeted us along the way when we entered Krajina. I had the impression that they were overjoyed to see anyone from Belgrade in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention now to the meeting you had with Mr. Martic at the police station. Can you please summarise that meeting for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: As I mentioned a short while ago, before meeting Martic, I had an idea as to how the defence was set up, and then I actually decided that I could help introduce some discipline into this defence. Perhaps it's important to mention one more thing: Very often, Sasa Medakovic said to me that among the defenders, quite a few people were injured because they did not use weapons professionally, because they did not maintain weapons professionally. And that is when I saw that there was a reason for me to get involved and to help bring into order this discipline. As for the meeting itself, it went on for about half an hour. Martic talked about his own problems, that they had firmly decided not to allow -- I mean, I remember a sentence he said to me. "We went to the beds of our great grandfathers where we slept over the past 600 years, and the next day we woke up not knowing whether we would live until next week." Well, that's it more or less. Well, he convinced me that there was indeed fear and that they were firmly resolved to remain there, not to be expelled, and I offered to help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you offered to help him, what was his response to that offer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure -- well, perhaps I can put it this way: In a way, he refused it. He said, "At this point in time, we need all sorts of things. We need money. We need equipment. We need political support. We need everything. We are endangered here, and also we are encircled." I left him my contact numbers, and he said that he would get in touch with me if he thought that he needed this kind of concrete help. So then we parted. This meeting did not take more than half an hour. He talked more than I did. To tell you the truth, I wasn't really all that interested in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what he had to say. What I said pertained primarily to the technical aspect as to how I could help, and my thinking at the time was that I should come there and organise a small course so that these unnecessary, unfortunate incidents would be prevented and so that this discipline would be brought into order properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, did you return to Belgrade that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the same evening, we returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Soon after you returned to Belgrade, did you set up a meeting with a member of the government?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Just a moment. Yes. Yes. I met with two men, with two men, and I would say that they were linked to the government. I don't know who you mean now. One is Sainovic, and the other one is -- my mind seems to have stopped. He was a member of parliament, the one I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you about your meeting with Mr. Sainovic first, and then perhaps you will recall the name of the other person. Can you please describe for us how the meeting with Mr. Nikola Sainovic came about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, at that time I met Mr. Sainovic through aeroplanes. Mr. Sainovic had built an airport in Bor, in the town where he had lived, and that is how I established contact with him. I think that in that period, he was some kind of Assistant Minister for Energy or something like that. But he was the only man -- he was the only man in some ministry, so I thought it would be smart to consult him, to tell him what I saw in Krajina and to ask him to lobby, if possible, at decision-making places so that I could get involved too, because I thought I could help, and I thought that I should help.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: This took place at the London Hotel in the centre of Belgrade. The meeting took about 15 minutes, as long as it took us to have a cup of tea, and this was a friendly conversation. He promised that he would get me in contact with some people. I don't know whether he did any lobbying on my part or not, but I did not have any further contacts with Mr. Sainovic regarding Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You mentioned another person that you spoke with. Do you recall the name now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Srba Milovanov. As I said, Srba Milovanov also has to with -- something to do with aviation; he is a pilot too. So this was more or less the route I could take. He was also a member of the SPO, the political party of the SPO. I joined that party too, although I was never active there. It was mainly for Srba and other friends of mine, because the opposition became popular then, and I liked the idea of an opposition, a strong opposition, and in principle, I've always been a member of the opposition until the present day. That is only thing I wish to say in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, when you met Mr. Milovanov, did he offer to introduce you to another member of the Serbian government?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He promised to get me in touch with Radmilo Bogdanovic. I had never known Radmilo Bogdanovic, I had never seen him except for a few pictures in the newspapers. However, there is something you have to understand so that the Tribunal will have an understanding of this: I knew very few people in Yugoslavia because I had just come from abroad. So some people who were highly recognisable to everybody else were just ordinary people to me and they didn't mean a thing to me. He promised that he would get me in touch with Radmilo Bogdanovic, and one day he called me and said, "You're going to have this meeting with members of the service."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, before you describe that meeting, did you ever have a meeting with Mr. Bogdanovic? And I'm talking about during this time period.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Not that I know of. Perhaps we met on that day, but I did not recognise him. And when Srba Milovanov took me to this meeting, there were many people wearing suits in front of the service building. So I do not remember having seen him too. But I don't think we talked about anything important. I really cannot remember whether I actually saw him then. I know that I saw him later, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, after you had the meeting with Srba Milovanov where he offers to introduce you to Mr. Bogdanovic and before you have this next meeting you are about to describe, did you return to the United States?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to wait a little before answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked, if you would, to pause between the question and answer, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you return to the United States during this period of time to complete your aviation training?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: After the meeting with the members of the service -- yes. Yes, you're right. You're right. I did return. I did return to America. Oh, I'm sorry. I'm really sorry. Twelve years is a long time, and during these 12 years many things happened around me. Please bear with me. I'm really trying to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, it's not so much important when you went to America. Do you remember when you returned again to Belgrade and what prompted you to return once again to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember very accurately when I returned. On the 9th of March -- or on the 10th of March, sorry. It was in the headlines all around the world that the tanks of the Yugoslav People's Army were in the streets of Belgrade. That very same moment, I reached a decision. I thought that I should stop what I was doing in America, and I thought that I should be in my town, just as I think that if tanks were to appear in the streets of Melbourne tomorrow, I would want to be there. That was my main motive. There was a big strike going on there, so I arrived in Belgrade perhaps on the 10th or possibly the 11th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, upon your return, did you once again meet with Mr. Milovanov, at which point he offered to introduce you to two other men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you're right. After my return -- I mean, let's get this in the right chronological order. It is only then that Milovanov took me to the service and introduced me to the people from the service, the Serbian service.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what people did he introduce to you at the Serbian state security service?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a group of people there. The only people I can remember are Franko Simatovic and Dragan Filipovic, Fico.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have a meeting with both of those men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: We did not spend much time in the building itself. We immediately went to the Metropole Hotel. That's where we had a conversation that took a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you summarise that conversation briefly and then I will ask you some specific questions regarding particular aspects of it. So please summarise that conversation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, I think that during this conversation, the members of the service, although they had been very well-informed about me, surprisingly well, I think that they tried to find out a lot more about me. They didn't discuss Krajina very much. Whenever I tried to change the subject to the Krajina, we always went back to me. I think that this was a period during which they tried to understand what it was that I actually wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you -- let me ask you this: In that meeting, who was the primary person asking you questions regarding what you wanted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Frenki Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he also ask you about what your intentions were in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe for us -- what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I briefly described my impressions regarding the situation in Krajina itself, and I told him that I thought that I could contribute, to put some order there and that in that way we would save a number of lives and strengthen the defence of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you were telling him that you could put some order there, could you be more specific about what type of programme or things you were planning to do.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: My plan was to form a training camp where anyone issued with any kind of weapon should go through this camp. He should be processed administratively, then be trained professionally so that it should be placed under some sort of control, because as I said, everything seemed somehow disorganised down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Mr. Simatovic ask you about your qualifications for running such a training camp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: He was quite well informed about that already, so we did talk about that too. And then he asked me whether I could put that down on paper and prepare some kind of a manual for the training.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you tell him in response to that question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I said of course I could and that that was really the first step that needed to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Prior to the end of the meeting, did Mr. Simatovic give you a number at which you could contact him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We exchanged our telephone numbers, and he said that I should call him once I had prepared the manual.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the end of the meeting, did he make any reference to his activities with respect to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that quite a lot of the things that he was trying to do in Krajina -- first he told me that all the things that we had discussed mustn't go any further. No one should know about it. And also, he said many of the things he was doing in Krajina, if his bosses were to learn about it, he would probably be arrested and dismissed. So he obliged me not to tell anyone about what we had discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, can you approximate -- you've told us that you returned to Belgrade on the 10th of March. How long after your return did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a matter of days. Very shortly after that, because already on the 4th of April, I went to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was this the first contact that you knowingly had with any member of the Serbian state security service?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, without any doubt it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After the meeting, did you set out to draft a training manual?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you contact Mr. Simatovic and tell him -- [B/C/S on English channel]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The translation seems to have been a bit confused. Let me ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After you completed the manual, did you contact Mr. Simatovic and tell him that you had completed the manual?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That somebody would come and pick it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did somebody come and pick it up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, someone did come to fetch it. I'm not sure whether it was Fico or another member of the service, but someone did come, took it, and took it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you hear from Mr. Simatovic after you had provided the training manual?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Things in Krajina were getting worse. The situation was deteriorating, and I firmly decided to go to Krajina, with their assistance or without it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did there come a time when you made the decision to go to the Krajina to attempt to do this training you had described in the manual?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sasa Medakovic lent me a helping hand, because he said, "Regardless of them, we really need you down there." He really appealed to me to come, and he promised to take care of me getting full support from Martic and Babic and the other people who were deciding down there in Krajina that these others were not all that important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, we're having problems with the interpretation, apparently. The interpreters are having difficulty. Could you pause after the question to give them time to catch up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. I'm sorry. I'm just not used to talking with the -- remind me as often as you can, just don't get upset with me because of it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We all have to get used to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I could make a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, if you would listen to the Serbian translation in your headset rather than responding to my English question. I know you understand both English and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: That confuses it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when did you make the decision to go down to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't hear anything now. It was on the 3rd of March. I was in contact with Sasa Medakovic who was already in Krajina, who literally pleaded with me to come to Krajina. Because Frenki hadn't called, I called him up and I told him, "I'm not going to wait any longer, I feel it is my duty to be down there, and I just wish to let you know that I'm going tomorrow to Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, the translation has come back that you're saying the 3rd of March. You've testified earlier that you didn't arrive back until the 10th of March. What is the date that you made this phone call to Frenki Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I beg your pardon. Not the 3rd of March, the 3rd of April. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Simatovic say when you made this phone call?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: First he was rather angry. He said, "You're trying to kill yourself," probably thinking that he would cool me off by taking such an approach or, rather, dissuade me. However, I insisted and I said that, "If I was afraid, I wouldn't go there. I really think that I am needed down there and that's something I can do, and I felt it necessary to call Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you up because we had already discussed it and to let you know." He said that he would call me later but that I shouldn't go down there under any circumstances without hearing from him first. I said once again if I didn't hear from him the next day, that I was going, I was leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have another conversation with Mr. Simatovic prior to going to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He called me up, and he said would I mind if he went with me because he had some business to attend to down there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Mr. Simatovic accompany you down to the Krajina when you went there to begin your training?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Frenki Simatovic went with me, Fico - I thought he was his driver at the time - and also Mark Lynch, who had come from England a couple of days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Mark Lynch is the person you've described as a fellow aviator that you knew prior to going to Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague with whom I had planned to set up a small charter company in Africa. The idea was that we would spend about three weeks in Krajina to set up the camp, to pass on some basics to them, and then to go on to Africa, because that had been my choice, to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the fourth person you said who was in the car, Fico, is that Filipovic who you had described earlier as meeting you with Simatovic at your initial meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened once you arrived in the Krajina in early April 1991. And I'd like you to focus on now just the day that you arrived with Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Simatovic drove me to Sasa Medakovic's house. He left me and Marko there. Then as far as I can recall, after all, it was 12 years ago, I can't remember all the minutest details, but Sasa Medakovic took me to Golubovic. I'm not sure whether Martic was already there or came later, but Martic was present when he introduced me to some guys. There were some 80, maybe 100 men there, I don't know the exact number, wearing different uniforms, various weapons ranging from hunting rifles to Kalashnikovs, diverse insignia and markings, and that's it. Martic introduced me as their instructor and told them to obey me. I was never formally appointed, but I took things seriously, and I took over command over Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was Golubic used for prior to you setting up a training centre there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was an abandoned, some sort of a youth hostel or a vacationing centre for youth, something like that, which was in a rather bad state of disrepair. And I immediately started putting things in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did you get funding to begin to build the camp and to conduct the training? How did you receive your funding?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, at first I received funds through the police station, Martic - not him directly but his assistants - and the commander of the Territorial Defence, I think his name was Dragisic, who supplied me with the military supplies. We were quite inventive. I immediately gave instructions for new uniforms to be prepared that were not reminiscent of JNA uniforms. Also berets. I wanted to develop a new image for those guys. The villagers from the surroundings would come on a daily basis to bring material. And shortly after that, once the unit started forming and lining up, assistance was coming from all over, from all over the world people would come bringing money and equipment. Much of it was not of any use, but he had much greater support than I really needed for this training camp to be started.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic also take care of the administrative part of these people who showed up at the camp regarding recording their names and their personal details?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I set up my own administration later on, but at first as I still hadn't formed my teams, all the people passed through the local police station, and from there, they were dispatched to me so that I received men literally from the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At this point in time, can you describe what, if any, relationship your training had with the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely none. Believe me that 60 per cent of my forces were kept on the alert for any possible clash with the JNA. The JNA, in those days, was pretending to be a peace force or a buffer zone between the Croats and the Serbs. They didn't like me at all. I had no contact with any single officer. It was only later, many months later, that I managed to establish my first contact with someone from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time after this initial training that you identified the most capable of your men and transferred them to the fortress in Knin for advanced training and training to be instructors themselves?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: That was my idea. I had expected to be able to establish an infrastructure, some sort of an administration to train the instructors and potential commanders and to leave that part of the territory. I had no greater plans than that in that period of time. After the training, the most capable ones or those who promised most I would select and transfer them to the fortress in Knin. And I was given permission from Babic. I know I waited quite some time for that permission to use the fortress. Babic gave me that permission, and that is where the Knindzas, as they were known, were formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Around this same time, did you begin to send out some of the men on reconnaissance and intelligence-gathering patrols and missions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as they were made fit for this work, they were sent out in patrols to collect intelligence information or to check out intelligence information that I was receiving from the local state security service in those days, though I didn't have too much trust in what they were doing so that I wanted to check out many of those pieces of information that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask now that a map, it's Prosecution Exhibit 389, tab 4, I'd ask that it be placed on the overhead projector. It is a photocopy of Prosecution Exhibit 336, pages 30 and 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, I'd ask you to take a look at that exhibit, and perhaps with the pointer could you -- could you -- first, let me ask you, were you asked to make some markings on a photocopy of a map, markings of places relevant to your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It may be better for you to look to your left, where the original is sitting on that projector. Is this the map that you marked with your own hand?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see Knin, Golubic --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to go --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: -- on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to go from left to right, pausing briefing on each place that you've circled and just describe the significance of each place.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: To the left is Skabrnja. It is a territory that I liberated or occupied, depends on the point of view, in 1993. Then comes Benkovac, which is close to Bruska where the Alpha training centre was formed in 1993. Knin, the capital of Krajina in those days. And Golubic, which was very close to Knin, where the first training centre was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I've finished with that exhibit, thank you. I'd like to ask you about some of the original members of your training programme. Are you familiar with the name Rade Bozic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Rade was one of the original trainees in Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After leaving your training organisation or your training camp, where did Mr. Bozic go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: After I was literally expelled from Krajina, the unit fell apart and a part of the unit that didn't wish to serve under Babic went to Belgrade. A part of the unit, or a part of those young men reported for service in the state security service where the JSO was being formed, the unit for special purposes of that service. Oh, I'm sorry, I got lost for a moment. Rade Bozic went there, but he didn't stay for long. After only a couple of days, I think, he left the Serbian service and went to the region of Bijeljina or Brcko where he said, I think, until the end of the war, and I think he's still living there until this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know the name of the person who commanded the forces in that area, the area around Bijeljina and Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: His nickname was Mauzer. I don't know his name for sure. I had one occasion to meet him. I would stay in his camp on my way to and from Knin. Once, rather. I think I spent the night there once, maybe twice, when there was a big storm, heavy snowing, something like that. I had to spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the second person I would ask you about is are you familiar with the person by the name of Zika Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him well. Zika Ivanovic was my favourite. A very witty man and an extremely brave combatant. I remember him because he was the first man I actually arrested, because on one occasion - I think this was in the press too - at the very outset my patrol arrested a Croatian policeman who was suspected of cutting off an old man's ear. And when Zika heard about it, he slapped him. That same moment, I disarmed Zika and put him in the cell next to this Croat. And I think that is how Zika made a name for himself, as being the first man I had arrested in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was he also known by another name, a nickname?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Crnogorac, Zika Crnogorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, at some point did your organisation actually participate in military-style operations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: You must understand. I think things have to be put in proper perspective. In those days, the Croatian forces were extremely aggressive, and the only capable combat unit up to a point, all this is relatively speaking, was the one in Golubic. On the other side, you had 30.000 Zengas, Croatian guards who had armoured vehicles. And I felt it necessary to return a blow somewhere, and one of the first operations was the attack on the garrison at Ljubovo which I had planned and which I commanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there a code name for that operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The operation was known as Osa, or Wasp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 389, tab 5, and I would ask you, Mr. Vasiljkovic, did you also mark a map indicating the location of Ljubovo? And I note for the Court this is pages 24 and 25 of Prosecution Exhibit 336.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you also mark a map in that way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did mark it. And if you look at the map, you will see that Ljubovo is literally in the middle of Krajina. It was a powerful Croatian garrison, and my aim was to remove them from there. There were no civilians in Ljubovo or anything like that. It was just a Croatian garrison, and it seemed to me to be a good target.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after the operation here, did there come a time when you intercepted a bus filled with members of Vojislav Seselj's party that were coming into the arena?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, from the very beginning - and I stand by that - that throughout the theatre of operations, no one could participate with weapons unless he was either within the service, the police, or the army. And I still abide by that. Seselj, or at least that is how they were introduced to me, had sent a bus of what -- they called themselves Chetniks, but I have to explain to give you a proper picture. The Chetniks that I saw arriving were Chetniks that were highly reminiscent of the Chetniks from Bulajic's film. Let me explain what I mean when I say that. After the Second World War, a well-known film director, Bulajic, directed partisan films presenting the Chetniks as dirty, bearded, drunk, disorderly, and literally a bus full of such people armed with -- prehistoric is the wrong word, but weapons from the Second World War; rusty snipers who they got from who knows where from, there were only two or three on the whole bus, with men who gave a very ugly impression, and he sent these men to Krajina. I decided, and this was my own independent decision at the time, that in my zone of responsibility, and I considered this to be my zone of responsibility because I had the greatest strength there at the time, that no party armies should be formed, and I feared that there might again break out a conflict between partisans and Chetniks, in quotation marks, the conflicts from the Second World War. I intercepted that bus. I ordered the occupiers of that bus to get off. I delivered a brief speech saying that we need only Serbs here, without any prefixes, and whoever doesn't feel he qualifies as such can go back. I collected all their party markings, their badges, and everything else. About 20 per cent of them returned to go back to Belgrade. I fed them, I gave them something to drink, and saw them off from Krajina. Those who remained, I had them shaved, bathed, uniformed, and I deployed them into other units so that they wouldn't operate as a whole. And I can tell you that throughout the period I was there, I had no problems with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, what do you mean by "intercepting"? Were they not sent to you originally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they were not sent to me. They were sent to Krajina to wage war. And I intercepted the bus because I received information from a local member of the state security service that the border of Krajina had been crossed by a busload of Seselj's volunteers and that they were heading towards Korenica. I put a barricade on the road, I stopped the bus, I took them all off the bus, disarmed them, sent 20 per cent of them back, and the rest of them I standardised in a sense and deployed them in the unit. I had a lot of conflict over this with Seselj, and that is my -- the beginning of my conflict with Seselj, which is still continuing. A couple of days ago I read an article where he mentions my name with certain accusations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, you sent these people back because you determined Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that they were unfit in their present condition or present state to participate in your activities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: As I explained, some of them physically were not capable. There were some old men, people with big stomachs and people who perhaps even mentally were not absolutely fit, and there were some who simply did not wish to take off their party insignias. So I adopted a very firm position that if anyone wanted to wage war in Krajina, they had to be part of either the security service, the police, or the JNA. To carry weapons, they had to be attached to one of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you said that you learned that they had crossed the border. Is that the border from the Republic of Serbia into the Krajina? Is that the border that you had learned that they crossed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is the border I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you were informed that they had crossed the border from Serbia into the Krajina, you said from the state security service. Which state security service told you that they had crossed the border?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: The local state security service. The state security service of Krajina, under the command of Dule Orlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you a specific question regarding your earlier testimony. I'm quoting from the transcript. You said: "Throughout the theatre of operations, no one could participate with weapons unless he was either within the service, the police, or the army." Now, you've just told us that the army, I believe, is -- you're referring to the JNA. When you said "service," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: The secret service, or the state security. It's one and the same thing. Somebody calls it the secret service, somebody calls it the state secure, but we're talking about one and the same thing same service.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've mentioned two state security services in your testimony here this morning; the Krajina state security service and the Serbian state security service. Which security service were you referring to when you said the "service"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that until the present day, there is no one who is organised and who has weapons in the territory of present-day Yugoslavia who is not a member either of the service or the police or the army. I'm saying that in principle, it was not possible to survive. I mean, now, why is this important? Your Honours, please give me just half a minute to explain this. I think this is very important. Many good men died believing that they were serving on the police force or in the army or in the state security service, and today some people are trying to wash their hands from them. While I was in Krajina, but I'm firmly convinced that this was true in any other theatre of war as well, that all people who were under arms had to be under the command either of the service or of the army or of the police. I do not accept that anyone, any unit, could have acted independently. Even Seselj's unit. I was there as a policeman and I took over control over that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you said "state security service," were you referring to the state security service of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: You know what? Four names. You had three, and I gave you a fourth name: Franko Simatovic, Dragan Filipovic, Mile Radonjic, and Jovica Stanisic. These are the only names of the Serb service that appear throughout the war throughout the territory of Krajina. I really cannot assist you as to what happened in Bosnia and Kosovo, but I was involved in what was going on in Krajina. There is not a fifth person that I'm aware of. I believe that their role in the Krajina is being overplayed here, and probably at that time this worked in their favour that this was overplayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let counsel ask the questions and try and answer them, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After this incident with Seselj's men, did there come a time when Mr. Stanisic himself paid a visit to the training facility in Knin at the fortress?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to put it that way, that he came to visit me, but he was in Knin. As far as I know, he had family somewhere near Knin, and of course he visited me too. I don't think that anyone would have come to Krajina then without visiting me. Your Honours, please bear in mind that in that period you could not buy a newspaper, even the simplest crossword newspapers, without seeing my name in the newspapers. So this was in the news all the time, my name, and I assure you that every day at least 200 people came to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that his only reason was to visit you, all I'm asking is did he pay a visit to the training facility at the fortress?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course he did pay that kind of visit, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who was present at the time of his visit? Can you name the other significant people that were present?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Frenki Simatovic was there then, then Martic. I think Babic was there too. But I know that later on, all of us together were at a luncheon at a nearby restaurant where a relatively informal conversation was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stanisic congratulate you on the success that you had in training and organising some of the men down in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes. Everybody who came down there congratulated me, him included.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to the battle of Glina. Can you please set the scene for us: What had happened in Glina at the end of June 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of June, 1991, I was on two-day leave in Belgrade when the Croatian attack against Glina took place. The Croats took the area. The very same moment, I quit my leave and I returned to Krajina. The taking of Krajina -- of Glina is something that badly affected the people in Krajina. They had just started getting some kind of self-confidence. The barricades started looking completely different. There was order and discipline throughout the area of Krajina. Some kind of infrastructure had started functioning, and so on and so forth, and then Glina fell. This was a great blow to Krajina, and I immediately started making plans as to how we could liberate that part of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In part of developing your plans, did you mount a reconnaissance mission to go to Glina and to assess what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I gathered sufficient information about the situation in the field, this was already a month later, perhaps the 26th of June. I went with a chosen 20 men. They had light infantry weapons. I went on this reconnaissance mission with the idea of charting a detailed plan as to how Glina should be freed. I consulted Martic about this, and he said, "If you think you can do it, just do it."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At this time, what -- from what you could tell, what was the JNA doing in the area of Glina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA was holding the line of separation between the Croat forces that had occupied Glina and the Serb forces of the Territorial Defence that held some kind of a defence line on the other side. But this was only in the inception, I mean this defence line. And this separation line would not have existed had it not been for the JNA there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Literally it is the JNA that held the separation line, and that is an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, during the course of this reconnaissance mission, did you make the decision that you would actually try to retake the town with a military operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, let me just paint a picture for you. At the time, we did not have any sophisticated methods of communication. My greatest fear was invariably if we would set out with major forces to liberate the town, that we could have great casualties on both sides, ours and theirs, and that it is very hard to command large forces with an army that was still so green. There was a situation in Glina when I decided to turn this reconnaissance mission into a mission for taking the town of Glina. Actually, my assessment was that the Croatian forces had had training that had been very similar to that that the Serb forces had. Not my forces, the Serb forces. And I believe that if I could break their command, the rest of their line would fall too. I was deeply convinced that that would happen. Their command was at the police station, and it was guarded by forces of the Yugoslav People's Army. I managed to win over a young lieutenant who was 20 years old, and he was probably impressed by Captain Dragan. He commanded a tank, and my assessment was that if I managed to win him over and to have him help me with that tank, that I, with my 20 men, that is to say with the total of 21 men, I would be able to take the police station and break the command of the Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, did you -- this young person, officer, did he feature in the plan that you devised for the retaking of Glina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. He had a very important role.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, could you, in a sentence or two, just summarise the basic plan for how you planned to retake Glina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I singled out a detail of four men headed by Sasa Medakovic, who I trusted the most then, and I sent them through the JNA-held line, to go to enemy territory and then to open fire from the enemy side with light weapons - rifles, that is - against Drobnjak's tank. That is the officer we mentioned. Drobnjak would know about this beforehand, and he would protect his men by putting them behind armour. And then by returning fire, he would break a machine-gun nest which was on a roof -- on the roof of the house right next door to the police station. That was the most dangerous part. I believed that after that a rapid attack would make it possible for us, in all the commotion, to take over command and to break the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you counting on the JNA being drawn into the battle to assist you in the retaking of Glina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I expected that their assessment would be that the Croats were firing at them and that they would then return gunfire. So it was no longer only my 20 men. Then I would also have tanks. And that seemed inconceivable at the time because I was counting on tanks as well. In my estimate, the whole operation was supposed to take about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the JNA initially begin to fire on the positions as you intended?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the chances are one in a million. When Sasa Medakovic opened fire from his automatic rifle, one bullet cut off the hydraulic barrel of the tank. So Drobnjak only managed to fire a single shell at the machine-gun nest. He couldn't shoot any longer. We were divided in five groups consisting of four men respectively. This was a very intensive attack. However, Grujica Boric, commander of these forces of the Yugoslav People's Army, took a microphone and ordered the tank crew to stop firing. He forbade them to shoot. And he said that this had nothing to do with the JNA, that this was a battle between Chetniks and Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
