utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, it's time for the break. Would it be fair to say that a rather lengthy battle then ensued between your men and the Croats of which you were ultimately victorious?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: The battle started exactly at 11.00, and we took the police station only at dawn the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did the Croat troops withdraw from the area of Glina after that battle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I attacked them from three sides, leaving the fourth side open, giving them the possibility to leave. Because it really wasn't possible for me to take so many prisoners with the number of men that I had. They retreated across the river, and this was left to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that a convenient place for the Chamber to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, after the battle of Glina, did your men -- or did you issue your men a distinctive garment that they wore from that point forward?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the participants in the battle for Glina had red berets. I obtained red berets for them. It was the only thing I had to give them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After the battle of Glina, was it your intention to return to Knin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On your way to Knin, did something occur?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we got close to Dvor na Uni, I was informed by a policeman from Dvor -- now, there is one thing that is very important for the Tribunal to understand. This was almost the fifth day that I got no sleep. Try to play chess for five days, let alone go through this kind of battle. When I arrived in Knin, I weighed 27 kilogrammes less than I weigh today, so you can imagine the state I was in. I am pointing this out because of what happened afterwards. So please understand, I was very tired. This is battle fatigue. That's right word for it, and I don't know the word for it in Serbian. I was so fatigued that I started vomiting. I was really in poor shape. When we arrived in Knin I received information that a group of armed Serbs had carried out a massacre in a hospital, I think the village's name is Strugar, and that at that moment they had taken the police station at Dvor na Uni. Please bear in mind that four men, that is to say 20 per cent of my 20 men, had been wounded. I did not have any possibility to carry out an investigation in the area. But since I saw that a group of armed men was holding the police station, with my own men I walked up to the station, I disarmed these men. I said to them that there were accusations that they had committed a massacre. I disarmed them, I put them in prison cells, I personally locked them up. At that moment, since people had already started complaining, rebelling, why are we arresting Serbs and so on and so forth, then some Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. group of JNA security men showed up. I can't remember who they were exactly, but they introduced themselves as being security men from the JNA. It was also announced that Martic would arrive. I kept these people in prison, and quite literally I deployed my own men as follows: They held the police station under siege. I did not allow anyone to approach the police station until Martic arrived. I handed the key of the prison over to him, and then I proceeded to Knin. And as I was leaving, I fell asleep after we had travelled 200 metres. Please understand that this was not within my area of responsibility. I was just passing there, but since I thought that I had the strength to deal with this, somebody had brought this accusation that a massacre had been committed, and I believe that I did everything within the powers of a single individual to deal with the situation. Are you happy with my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vasiljkovic, I want to ask you, were there other occasions when you arrested Croat police and similarly turned them over to the custody of Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Croat police?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not talking about this incident at all, but were there other occasions when your men on patrol apprehended either Croat police or other people who were then subsequently turned over to Milan Martic as prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were arrests. I don't remember how many, but they were always handed over to the police station. Not to Milan Martic personally, but this was the protocol; if we arrested anyone, we were to hand them over to the police station in Knin. The Red Cross was there. Within 24 hours, we were duty-bound to hand them over to the Red Cross. So they were under Red Cross supervision. I don't remember the number involved, how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that Prosecution Exhibit 389, tab 6, be placed on the overhead projector. And this is another map, a photocopy of Prosecution Exhibit 336, pages 20 and 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The question I have for you, Mr. Vasiljkovic, is is this another map that you marked a particular location on relevant to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the town of Glina that we discussed a short while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to take, I believe it's a green pen in front of you, and I would ask you to circle the town of Dvor, the town where you just described this incident. And look over to your left where the original is on the overhead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I'd ask the director to zoom out a bit and focus on the lower portion of the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you returned to the fortress in Knin, were there members of Babic's Territorial Defence present at the fortress?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. To my astonishment, and I think this is important for you to understand, the fortress literally became a symbol of the defence of Krajina. This was a place where guards stood at attention for hours, where flags were flying, where everything was tidy, clean, and it really looked like a proper military. It looked like a command post. When I returned, to my astonishment, in the fortress I found members of the Territorial Defence who were unkempt, unshaven, dirty. And all of this happened while I was waging the battle for Glina. So at that moment when I saw that, I ordered them to leave the fortress. They told me that they were at the fortress on Babic's orders. I said to them that they should find another place then and clean it up and put it in order and not use the place that we had cleaned up and put in order. So that's when the first clash actually occurred between Babic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljkovic, did there come a time a few days after that that Frenki Simatovic showed up at the fortress?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was having a meeting with my staff. It was a regular-type meeting that I held, and Frenki Simatovic walked in. He was quite upset. There is a detail that I cannot recall exactly, but I'm going to try to convey the gist of it to the Tribunal. At this lunch where Jovica was, there was an informal conversation as to whether it was Martic or Babic - I can't remember who was saying this - but anyway, it was my understanding that Martic would lead the defence of Krajina and that Milan Babic would lead Krajina's policies. I wasn't that interested in it at the time, so I cannot recall all details, but my understanding was that that was the division of responsibilities. Then Frenki Simatovic, when he walked in, he sat next to me and he said to me semi-audibly that it seems that there were big problems that had cropped up, that Babic was not respecting the agreements he had with Martic, and let me be quite cautious. I mean, I should be quite cautious. I mean, right in the middle of that conversation -- I can't remember how he finished that conversation, but right in the middle of this conversation, at the door of this meeting room where I held meetings - this was my command post and that room was about as big as this room is - at a big table, there were about 30 officers sitting with me, and I sat at the head of that table, Babic walked in, and we were all astonished that he walked in because we did not expect him to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what happened after Mr. Babic walked into the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: When Babic walked in, Frenki stopped talking and he simply left the room, walking by Babic. Babic sat right next to me in the seat that he had taken. When I received all this information and also in addition to everything that I experienced when I came to the fortress when I saw his men who had taken the fortress, I simply proceeded, ignoring Babic. I was addressing the officers, and I said, "Guys, I don't know what is going on over here, but it's obvious that politicians are yet again going to ruin what we've been doing so far. It may easily happen that I will be replaced from this position or that you will not be under my command." I felt duty-bound to say something to these men, as to what would happen if I were no longer there. And I said to them, "I really don't know who I can trust any more around here. The only man so far who never betrayed me or cheated me is Frenki Simatovic, so listen to what he has to say." So it was along those lines. That was the context. Frenki was not present when I said that, but Milan Babic was present. Milan Babic, when he heard what I was saying about him, simply got up and left the room, quite shaken or perhaps frightened. I imagine it was not all the same to him when he realised how I was talking about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, in saying that to your men, was it your intention that, should you be replaced or removed, that they then look to Frenki Simatovic for their instruction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I mean, I didn't have anybody of my own there. When I say "of my own," I'm saying that I was the only person from Belgrade in that camp, and I sort of felt that Frenki Simatovic was the person closest to me. I thought literally that whatever may happen, he as an intelligence person will have the best information as to what was going on. I didn't say they should address them or subordinate themselves to him but they should simply listen to what he had to say, because quite realistically in that period, I did not have much choice and he was the only person I could trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After you addressed your men, did you at some point later in that day go and speak with Frenki Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that, I went out. I got into my jeep and I started searching for Simatovic. I found him. I asked him to sit down and tell me what was going on. He was very upset.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: He said to me that he was not sure, that there was only one thing that was certain - I'm sorry, I beg your pardon - but that Babic was an army whore. He meant that he was playing games with the army and that he did not want to see us there, that our presence troubled him in that respect. And then he said to me that I had to go to Belgrade to report to Jovica Stanisic because Jovica Stanisic would have a lot more information. Now, please bear in mind that I had just returned from the battle for Glina. As I mentioned at the outset how meaningful the loss of Glina was to the Serbs, you can well imagine what the liberation of Glina meant. As Frenki said, I'm not sure whether they want to give you a decoration or to dismiss you, but on your way to Belgrade, be very careful, take a lot of security people with you, and make sure that nobody knows when you're leaving and when you're arriving. When I arrived in Belgrade, since I really didn't have that much time in Krajina to follow the media, and there were hardly any in Krajina, it is only then that I realised how much the media had highlighted me in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, it would be helpful to have a date for these activities. The original taking of Glina was on the 28th of June. I don't think we've had a date since then. I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've referred to the 28th of June as the time when the Croats took Glina. Can you fix the date that you then -- your battle for Glina, when was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly a month later. The 28th of July. On the 30th of August, I was already in Krajina -- sorry, in Knin. And on the 4th of August, I went to Belgrade -- or, rather, on the 3rd of August, in the evening. So all of these things that were happening in Knin were happening between the 1st and the 3rd of August. Within those two days, to be quite precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did you go to Belgrade and see Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to Belgrade. I stayed with my friends. I called Stanisic. I phoned Stanisic using the telephone number that Frenki had given me, and Mr. Stanisic appeared at my home or, rather, at the home of my friends where I was staying. He brought me a pistol, CZ99 with his signature, as a present, and he congratulated me on the battle for Glina. He asked me to go out for a walk with him because he did not want to talk in the presence of my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, I omitted to ask you one question about the time that Mr. Stanisic went down to the fortress and had lunch. During your conversation with Mr. Stanisic at that time, did you ever request from him whether there was any -- whether you could receive any assistance for the work you were doing down in that area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but I'm almost sure I did, because I asked help from anyone who came there. And of course I would ask such an important man, like Jovica Stanisic was, for help too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My apologies. I want to draw your attention back to the 4th of August, 1991. Did you go for a walk with Mr. Stanisic on that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Chamber what occurred during that walk with Mr. Stanisic on the 4th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, almost apologetically Stanisic said to me that some very dirty business was going on in Krajina, that I probably unconsciously got involved in politics and that I shouldn't go back there any more, and if I tried, that he would be forced to put a barrier down, which meant literally that he had forbidden me to go back to Krajina. I didn't know then. I asked him -- well, he said, "I don't know whether it's temporary." I remained convinced -- well, I don't know whether my replacement was temporary or definite. Things were the way they were, and I asked him what I should do, and he said, "Go to Bor. That's the place where Nikola Sainovic lives. Then somebody will meet you there and take care of you until we think of where you could help the most."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you question Mr. Stanisic regarding who was requesting or who was forbidding you from going back to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, he said, "I can't tell you much. You will understand that." But he said, "This is coming from the very top." My understanding was that this should have either been the Minister of the Interior or President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you in fact go to Bor in Serbia for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My escort that had escorted me to Belgrade stayed behind in Belgrade, and I with a member of the service whom I didn't know, went to Bor, and they put me up in one of Tito's villas. I stayed there for seven to ten days, roughly, waiting for someone to get in touch with me and to tell me what I should do next.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did anybody ever come and inform you about what you should do next?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I started to think that I had literally been removed from the scene in a nice way. I became rather nervous, and one evening I saw Milan Babic's interview on television. When one of the spectators asked him, "Can you tell us anything about Captain Dragan?" And Babic answered, and I quote, "Captain Dragan is a mercenary who was hired to do a job. He's done it, he has been paid for it, and he's left on his way." When I heard that, I really became mad with fury.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you do in response to seeing that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: As I already had my doubts before leaving Belgrade that something was being done behind my back, I fixed some signals so if I felt unsafe, the men who had secured me as far as Belgrade would come and assist me. So I called up those men, headed by Sasa Medakovic, who is a member of the service from Krajina, they came to Bor. I got in touch with my friend, lady friend, Klara Mandic who was influential in social circles at the time, and asked her to be kind enough to arrange a press conference for me in the international press centre. I wanted to tell the public that I hadn't been paid for it, that I hadn't received any money for it, that I hadn't left but that I had been expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljkovic, did you eventually conduct such a press conference where you fully aired your positions regarding the reasons why you were in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I first of all scheduled the press conference in the international press centre, but several hours later, they told me that the hall was booked, reserved, and that it would continue to be reserved indefinitely so that I would never get a chance to have my press conference. So Klara said, "You can organise a press conference under any tree, and all the journalists will come. I suggest that you do at it at my friend's who is director of a hotel in Kragujevac, and don't worry, all the reporters will come." That is what I did. And with Klara and my security escort, we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. went to Kragujevac and I held a press conference there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Around this same time, did you begin an initiative to assist the widows of war victims or -- and casualties of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, it was like this: I had lost trust in the contact I had with the Serbian service once I left Bor, and to make the situation clear to you, I was literally guarded by two members of the State Security Service of Serbia. When my guys arrived, I said, "I am leaving," so that I left though they didn't want me to. So it wasn't with their approval. By then, I had lost trust in the service as far as I personally was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you -- I will ask you in detail about the Captain Dragan fund tomorrow, but could you just give us one or two sentences, was this the period of time which you founded the Captain Dragan fund?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I founded the fund after this press conference, because I realised that I obviously would no longer be included in the armed forces, that somebody had his reasons not to engage me, and I wanted to take advantage of this unbelievable popularity. And it must be difficult for you who are not from Serbia to understand how great that popularity was. It was greater than any soccer player, any pop star. It was really very great, and I wanted to take advantage of it to do something useful, and of course at the same time to be in the centre of events in Serbia. So I said to myself, if they won't let me be Milos Obilic, I've decided to be Kosovka Devojka. Milos Obilic would be something like Lawrence of Arabia, and Kosovka Devojka would be something like Mother Theresa.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will ask you in greater detail about the fund tomorrow morning. Can you describe for us what happened to the men that you left in the Krajina now that you were in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Some of those men were already in Belgrade at my side and securing me. My situation was rather difficult. I didn't know -- even know the language too well at the time. I didn't even know who was who. I could just read between the ranks in the newspapers. Klara Mandic was a major source of information that I trusted. So I was really at the time totally confused with respect to the overall situation. As for my men, I felt a moral obligation towards them -- [In English] I see myself now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He's pushed a button accidentally on the console.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] I think it's okay now. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So can you tell us, just briefly, where did they go? The ones that were in Belgrade, did they go to join any other organisation? What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure whether I called him or he called me. I don't remember the details, it's been a long time. Anyway, it was Frenki Simatovic who told me that he had launched an initiative for the service to form a unit, an armed unit in the military sense, and that those guys who didn't want to stay in Krajina would be welcome in that unit. Of course I accepted that wholeheartedly, and I offered to initiate the formation of such a centre or training camp and everything that that entailed. Frenki promised or, rather, the arrangement was that this time one should not act in an improvised manner but that we get all the documents from the state first, that my status must be defined, that I must be an employee of the service, and that all the guys who joined must also be employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where was this? Where was Frenki Simatovic going to set up this armed group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a hunting lodge at Fruska Gora. It's a mountain not far from Novi Sad in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The group that Mr. Simatovic was referring to, is that the same group that was being honoured in the ceremony that we saw in the videotape earlier today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the men wearing camouflage uniforms were veterans belonging to that group. Of course some were killed, like Sasa Medakovic, who isn't there. But yes, in principle, most of them were from that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Around this time, were you instrumental in the purchase of uniforms that would then later be worn by this group during their operations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As this was a unit in the process of formation, in those days hundreds of men applied daily who wanted to get close to me. One of them was Dafina Milanovic, a banker in those days, who offered to assist the people in Krajina. I told her that a unit was being formed which needed equipment and that if she wanted to help, she could help us purchase that equipment because such equipment cannot be found in Yugoslavia. She agreed, and she approved 1 million German marks for me. I never received that money in cash, I just linked her to a German merchant of military equipment. His name was Robert Keizer. I made a list of supplies - helmets, flak jackets, night sights, camouflage uniforms, boots - for roughly the strength of a company. And these supplies reached me, I took them to Fruska Gora, and I dressed the young men who were gathering gradually at Fruska Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For those of us unfamiliar with the size of a military company, can you approximate the number of people that would be.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: This will probably be cropping up. If we say one platoon, numbers 30 men. If we say a company, that's about 100 to 150 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to describe the appearance of these uniforms as being similar to the types of uniforms that members of NATO forces would wear in their operations? And if not, could you explain the differences.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were identical to the uniforms worn by the American military. They were purchased in America, and they do not differ in any way from the uniforms worn by American soldiers before the Kuwait conflict in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, although they appeared like these American uniforms, they had no emblems or any kind of markings which erroneously identified them as American uniforms, did they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about camouflage combat uniforms that don't have any markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were the subject of threats while you were in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. An incident occurred shortly after or during this process, but shall I finish the previous story so as to avoid leaving things hanging in the air? I didn't get the conditions promised, I didn't get the documents, I didn't get what I had asked for, and I abandoned that project. I left Frenki with those men and that equipment, and I devoted myself to the fund. Now, yes, at one point in time I clashed very seriously with the security service. For someone listening, this might sound like a cheap American thriller. The details are the following. I'll try and be brief. Vojislav Seselj, with a pistol in hand, threatened students at Belgrade's Faculty of Law. The students got armed in the centre of Belgrade and they came to see me, asking protection from me. When I heard that in my town, at my university, children were getting armed, I was seriously concerned. I went to the campus, of course I disarmed the children, took the equipment from them, and said the following: "In this country there is a Ministry of Justice and a Ministry of the Interior, and if you wish to file charges against Seselj, you must go through them." They said, "They won't receive us." So I said, "If they won't receive you, I will lead demonstrations against Seselj with you," never thinking for a moment that the two ministers wouldn't receive them. Unfortunately, they were not received by these mentioned ministers, and the children, the students, announced demonstrations in front of the parliament building. Seselj was already inside at the time. I asked Radmilo Bogdanovic to start proceedings to strip Vojislav Seselj of his immunity so that proceedings could be instituted against him because of this incident with the students, and Radmilo Bogdanovic promised to do that. So I stopped the strike, the protest. But in the meantime, several thousand people had gathered in front of the parliament. That is just the introduction to the conflict. A day later, two members of the state security service came to my office and asked me to follow them for an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Can you please help us with what time, what time period are we talking about when these two men arrived at your office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot remember. It was probably the autumn of that year. But the date can be found because of this incident with Seselj which was published in all the media. But really, it was a long time ago, and I can't remember the date. But it was that same year. Probably in the autumn of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, who were the two men that came to visit you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: One was Dragan Filipovic, the other was Milan Radonjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And for whom did they work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: They worked for the state security service of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: They took me to a raft near the river, and they explained to me that it was very difficult for them to say what they were going to say but that I had entered certain waters that I did not understand, and they asked me to leave Yugoslavia. They told me that they had accepted to carry out this assignment because if someone else had done it, they would have probably done it differently, and I took this to be a threat. They asked me how much money I needed to disappear from Yugoslavia for five years and never to crop up again anywhere. I said, "For five years, I need about $250.000, about 50.000 a year to seek shelter somewhere in an island in the Indian Ocean and to wait for everything to blow over." Of course I wasn't pleased with their request to leave the country, but also I was not ready to clash with the state security service. I had no motive to wage war against my own country. So we agreed that we would see each other again the next day and that Fico would try to ensure the sum I had requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, before this meeting ended, did you ask where this order came from, where this directive came that you should leave the country?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: The answer was very similar to the one given by Jovica Stanisic earlier on. "It is coming from the top," they said, and no one can have any influence regarding that decision. I had to leave the country. I told this story to a friend of mine, a journalist that I trusted absolutely, and after quite a lot of convincing, he persuaded me that we go to see Nedjelko Boskovic, who was then chief of the intelligence or counter-intelligence service of the JNA, I'm not quite sure which, counter-intelligence, yes, and he told me that he knew Nedjelko Boskovic very well, that he was a man of his word, and that if I insisted that he was to keep it to himself, he would. So I trusted the chief of the military intelligence with this information, and he said the following: "You are a citizen of this country and no one can expel you. But if you accept their offer, what could easily happen is that you'll be found somewhere outside the country, dead, and a report could appear in the paper saying that you had been killed in a Mafia settling of accounts, and I think it's very dangerous." Then I asked, "What do you think we should do?" Then he said, "Let us try and listen in to conversations." And I did so. I mounted it in my hotel. I went to a meeting with Filipovic. I provoked him to repeat what he had said the previous day. Of course I didn't bring those tapes, though they are in my possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The record is unclear. What was translated was that you were going to listen in to conversations. What exactly was decided to do with respect to future meetings with these men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: To begin with, Nedjelko Boskovic proposed that we just tape these threats of theirs. That was the purpose of the taping, of the recording. And that then he would consider and analyse those threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At some later point, did Frenki Simatovic come to you, to your house, and request those tapes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: If you give me another 30 seconds to finish the story. I gave this tape to Nedjelko Boskovic. A transcript was done, and several days later Frenki Simatovic came to see me. He came to see me. That was your question, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know what Mr. Boskovic did, or General Boskovic did with the transcript of the tapes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: He told me what he would do. He said that he would copy them and take it to Jovica Stanisic and that my best protection was that threat. Because if anything were to happen to me, nobody would be able to free the service of the responsibility for this. But he asked me not to make too much noise about it, not to publicise the whole thing, not to make it public, and that he would see what should be done next. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you take a look at the monitor now, and I'd ask that it be switched to the appropriate position. I'm going to ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 389, tab 7, which will appear in front of you. If you need it enlarged or you want to see the hard copy, we can provide that. Do you recognise the signature on the bottom of the page of Prosecution Exhibit tab 7?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: It says Marko Njegovanovic. I never saw his signature, but I have no reason to doubt that that is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us who he was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was the commander of the command of the town of Belgrade, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you to read the last sentence in the first paragraph that appears before you and the entire last paragraph, which refers to you and then I'd ask you to comment on it. If you would read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] I have a reflection here from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the light. I shall have to get up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We'll hand up a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would be easier perhaps. "In accordance with Article 137 of the Rules of Procedure of the People's Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, we are giving the following answer: It is known that the armed forces of Yugoslavia consist of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence. Their interrelations are precisely defined in legal and other regulations valid. Commanding in the armed forces is based on the principles of the unity of commanding in regards with the use of the forces --" is that what you wanted me to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Actually, it would be fine if you started with the last sentence of that very paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think you've given me the wrong document. Aha. I see. I'm sorry. It's on the second page. "Volunteers that make war in the territory of Srpska Krajina are within the TO units and they are under unique command of the armed forces and so far there have not been any major problems. "As far as we know, Captain Dragan has no special personnel that he's training or commanding in those territories now. It is known that earlier he was engaged in training the members of the TO of Krajina, so-called Knindzas, and that those formations are fighting in coordination with the JNA. Based on this -" this is not quite clear - "there are no indications to doubt whether there is enough cooperation which is expected from these units."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is the date of that document, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: The 20th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please comment on the veracity of that document as it pertains or describes the relationship you had with Territorial Defence forces.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VASILJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, I don't see anything incorrect there. I've already spoken about it and I think this only confirms what I've already said. Are there any additional questions in this connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Chamber would still like 15 minutes at the end of today's session, this would be a convenient place to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Mr. Vasiljkovic, we will adjourn now. Could you be back, please, at 9.00 tomorrow morning when we'll continue the evidence. Thank you. If you'd like to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will begin by dealing with the matters we can deal with in open session, which is the evidence of Mr. Davies. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, we had actually filed a subsequent motion in relation to this witness that may, I think, meet the concerns of the amici, because in the subsequent motion dated the 21st of January of this year, we had indicated that in relation to several paragraphs - and these are the paragraphs related to the defence in Dubrovnik and the targeting of civilian objects - the witness would testify, testify live, and only in relation to the other paragraphs which are corroborating actually only the shelling of Dubrovnik as such and some other background aspects, we would recommend 92 bis, and I think that meets the concerns of the amici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness is a journalist who came to Dubrovnik, describes shelling which we have heard much evidence about already, but then describes matters, paragraphs 32 to 42, which are in dispute as to the role of the civilian defenders. What is proposed that -- Mr. Milosevic, what's proposed is that those paragraphs are the subject of live evidence, the rest of the statement be admitted under Rule 92 bis, there being no reference to you or your acts and conduct, and that you then have the opportunity to cross-examine. Anything you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only to point out once again that I'm categorically opposed to the application of Rule 92 bis, because to date, it has been proven that the application of this role is -- rule is quite inadequate for establishing the facts that you wish to have established here. I believe that it is quite inappropriate to apply Rule 92 bis in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it's quite clear the accused is opposed to any admission of evidence in written form and seeks viva voce testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's very plain he's against it as a matter of principle, but we have to apply our Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a discretionary matter for the Trial Chamber, so notwithstanding even that the criteria may fit, it's still a matter that the Trial Chamber has to use its discretion upon. Every statement, in many respects, is a unique statement that gives different detail upon incidents, and the accused's position is quite clearly that it provides less opportunity for him to highlight discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We understand that, Mr. Kay, but we want your submissions as amicus, not a repetition of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The issue here that one as to consider is the Galic decision. We've got 7(3), issue of command responsibility, and just to highlight the words from that decision which we've quoted in the written document put before the Court at paragraph 23: "There is often a short step from a finding that the acts constituting the crimes charged were committed by subordinates to finding that the accused knew or had reason to know of the crimes." And the judgement goes on to say: "It comes to a position no way he couldn't have heard about it." So that's the position that the Appeals Chamber were highlighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But here there is an issue as to whether this accused was in charge of the JNA or not. That's a matter which is in dispute, is it not, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it's not a position in which in Galic you had a commander, he was the commander of the Sarajevo siege. So he was the commander of the troops. Here we have other issues of linkage and command responsibility, not a direct responsibility as they have in Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But it's the acts of the JNA in allegedly shelling Dubrovnik, which is the issue here. It's all tied up with those events surrounding Dubrovnik and who was giving the orders and what would have been known about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But the issue is, the crucial issue we're going to have to determine here is whether there was a connection between the accused and the JNA. That's one of the crucial issues in the case in this regard. But you seem to be against the application of Rule 92 bis in the same way as the accused. You're just against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're putting forward his position on that, and in relation to it, we provide an alternative argument that permits his cross-examination of witnesses called under 92 bis. If the discretion of the Court is to be exercised in favour of admitting evidence in a cumulative form in that way, our position is that he should at least have a right to cross-examine, taking again the approach of the Trial Chamber throughout this trial to date, so that those issues can be dealt with by him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a case in which there will be an opportunity to cross-examine in any event. Whichever way we rule, there must be cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are no provisions in the Rule which prevent this statement being admitted under Rule 92 bis. It does not relate to the acts and conduct of the accused. It is not sufficiently proximate, as alleged, to him to require it to be excluded under the Rule. We will order that the statement be admitted under Rule 92 bis but that paragraphs 32 to 42 be given live, the accused to be able to cross-examine the witness. I think the other two matters have to be dealt with in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the witness General Mangan, I think we can remain in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I didn't know we were going to -- you want to deal with him too?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, because it's actually the same argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the same argument. Do you want to call him soon?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Actually, he is scheduled at the moment for next week. For next week, and this is why -- and because it's a very similar situation, I would think it should be dealt with also now. And we have also in that same filing that related to Mr. Davies, we had suggested that General Mangan should be heard also on all issues that are here crucial and in dispute; that is the defence situation in Dubrovnik and also the reasoning behind the attack on Dubrovnik, the artillery operations, the conduct should be viva voce and only those corroborating other matters should be 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I don't think we -- given the time constraints, we must deal with those other two matters. We'll deal with him tomorrow, if you would remind us. We'll come back to him. Are we in private session? All right. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of February, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 25
